newsitem.title: USA: S&P says Calif. county portfolios focus on safety.
newsitem.headline: S&P says Calif. county portfolios focus on safety.

text.p: California counties are shifting their investment strategies, sacrificing some yield for increased safety and liquidity, according to a report Monday by Standard & Poor's Corp.

Based on a review of the portfolios of 22 California counties, S&P concluded that they all have credit characteristics that "offer adequate protection for the investment of local government operating funds."
The following county portfolios were detailed Monday in the rating agency's CreditWeek Municipal newsletter:

* Alameda County. Its portfolio is now less than 1 percent invested in potentially more volatile derivative securities. The county participates in a lending program that leverages about 15.6 percent of the portfolio, but matches maturing securities to the loans. Liquidity is "very strong," with 55 percent of investments maturing within 90 days, S&P said.

* Monterey County. Its pooled investment portfolio displays a high degree of liquidity, with 52 percent maturing in 90 days or less and 28 percent consisting of overnight funds. This liquidity, plus the 100 percent mandatory status of the pool participants, "provides a satisfactory level of security for the investment of local government operating funds," S&P said.
The weighted average maturity of the portfolio is 238 days. About 20 percent of the portfolio consists of U.S. agency structured notes, mostly maturing in 1998, S&P said.

* Placer County. The pool's market value has strengthened to 98.3 percent of book value. Liquidity continues to improve, with 65 percent of the portfolio maturing within 90 days, up from 46 percent a year ago, S&P said.

The Placer County pool continues to hold a significant position in potentially volatile derivatives -- 42 percent of the portfolio's market value as of March 31, S&P said. The rating agency added, however, that these securities will be held to maturity, and will pay off at par.

* San Diego County. Its portfolio continues to improve, with its average weighted maturity now down to 506 days from 703 days at April 30, 1996, S&P said. The market value of the pool remains 5.0 percent below the book value as of March 31, 1997, the rating agency said.

Short-term liquidity is also improving, although just 17.2 percent of the San Diego County portfolio matures within 90 days, S&P said. The county's holdings of less liquid and more volatile structured notes stands at 31.65 percent of the portfolio's book value.
* San Mateo County. Its portfolio is the longest of the county portfolios evaluated, at three years weighted average maturity, S&P said.

* Solano County. It continues to reduce its holdings of more volatile derivatives, S&P said. These securities comprise 30 percent of the portfolio, down from 45 percent in June 1996 and 57 percent in June 1995, the rating agency said. The portfolio does not contain any leverage.

* Sonoma County. Its portfolio includes a 30 percent position in derivatives, but less than 10 percent of the securities could be classified as potentially volatile, S&P said. All are backed by the U.S. Treasury or U.S. agencies and most mature within one year. The portfolio is liquid, with 29 percent of investments maturing within 90 days and 54 percent in a year.
